#1: FACT-CHecking APPROACHES
Why does fact-checking matter, and is it effective? Fact-checking, just like journalism, is
about informing audiences about the truth. Even if it is a limited audience, or if people
disagree, calling out disinformation attempts to hold people and institutions accountable.
Sometimes fact-checking efforts are picked up by larger outlets and reach wider audiences,
but even if they are, publishing fact-checking is only the first step in an incremental process.
When watchdogs expose untruths, this can become a resource for public action, particularly
when mobilized by political campaigns or social movements. They can also identify trends
and help trigger an institutional response by regulators, courts, or legislators.
In the last few years, fact-checking organizations have become more effective and grown
tremendously. The Reporter's Lab hosts a database of reporting projects that regularly
debunk political misinformation and viral hoaxes. As of 2019, the database counts 210 active
fact-checking organizations in 16 countries, up from 59 sites tallied in 2014.175
Bringing these organizations together, the International Fact Checking Network provides
resources, monitors trends, and promotes basic standards for fact-checking organizations
through its code of principles.176 Many of these organizations work in USAID program
countries; it is worth reaching out to them when developing disinformation programming. A
few examples of fact-checking organizations are included in Annex 3: Emerging Solutions.
The Effectiveness of Fact-Checking
The effectiveness in fact-checking is the subject of numerous studies. These studies have
often produced contradictory results. In one key study, researchers from three universities
teamed up to analyze the results of the studies and determine the effectiveness of fact-
checking across research studies. The resulting study helps shed some light on the fact-
checking landscape and the ins and outs of what works in fact checking. It found that:
USAID.GOV
DISINFORMATION PRIMER | 45

• Fact-checking with graphical elements is less effective than those without,' and simple
messages are more effective when informing the public on false information. 178
• Fact-checking an entire statement rather than individual elements is more effective.
• When fact-checking, debunking an idea is more effective when it is refuting ideas in line,
as opposed to, a person's own ideologies.179
While it is important to consider the limitations of fact-checking—it is not a panacea for all
disinformation—fact-checking is highly prized by many people and is especially important for
media outlets and others who are in the business of investigating and reporting facts.
#2: REDIRECTION METHOD
The Redirect Method primarily relies on advertising using an online advertising platform such
as Google AdWords, targeting tools and algorithms to combat online radicalization that
comes from the spread and threat of dangerous, misleading information.
The method redirects users through ads who seek to access mis/disinformation online to
curated YouTube videos uploaded by individuals around the world that debunk these posts,
videos, or website messages. The Redirect Method, a method used to target individuals
susceptible to ISIS radicalization via recruiting measures, is being adapted in several
countries to combat vaccine hesitancy and hate speech. 180 The method was developed by a
collaboration among private and civil society organizations and is documented on The
Redirect Method website. The collaboration provides 44 steps in the organization of an
online redirect campaign. Other examples of the use of redirection are being employed by
groups around the world.
#3: DEBUNKING AND DISCREDITING
The Global Engagement Center (GEC) at the U.S. Department of State recommends a
combined debunking and discrediting approach, which is explained in GEC Counter-
Disinformation Dispatches #2: Three Ways to Counter Disinformation and GEC Counter-
Disinformation Dispatches #4: What Works in Debunking.
Key points include:
• A "counter-brand" approach, which involves discrediting the "brand"—the credibility and
reputation—of those making false allegations.
• Highlighting false claims seen as obviously absurd and particularly offensive and
objectionable by target audiences
• Changingthe frame from the false allegation to the misdeeds and lack of credibility of
those spreading disinformation
• Creating moral outrage: truth is a sacred value; spreading vicious disinformation violates
this sacred value, creating moral outrage.
• Recognizing that the mind often reasons by associations rather than logic.
See the GEC Counter-Disinformation Dispatches for more details.

#5:
LEGAL AND POLICYMAKING ADVOCACY
As information pollution and disinformation begin to affect the ways in which democracies
function, governments have become aware of the importance of combating false information
online. While there is government support to find ways to combat the information disorder,
democracies are struggling to find the best way to regulate disinformation online. There is an
inherent contradiction between the democratic ideal of free speech and the regulation of
online content. Despite this, some governments have been developing policies that are
intended to combat the spread of hate speech and disinformation, while simultaneously
working hard to preserve free speech online.
However, when democracies pass new laws to curb the spread of disinformation,
authoritarians can adopt these laws as yet another tool to criminalize free expression. So,
there is great risk of making the situation worse by regulating online speech. A very clear
example is Germany's NetzDG law (requiring social media to take down harmful content)
that was later adopted by Russia, Venezuela, and other countries as a means of silencing
opposition. 184
The Advisory Network to the Media Freedom Coalition, a group of 17 national, regional, and
international organizations, delivered a statement at the ministerial meeting of the 2020
Global Conference for Media Freedom and put forward the following guidance to support
legal and policymaking advocacy that seeks to deal with the disinformation problem:
USAID.GOV
DISINFORMATION PRIMER | 47

• Respect media freedom while tackling disinformation.
• Efforts to combat disinformation and "fake news" must start with governments, which
should not criminalize this but also must commit to not perpetuating disinformation and
take news.
• Counter the criminalization of journalism through so-called anti-fake news laws and anti-
terrorism laws.
• Promote media engagement in countering disinformation by expanding access to
information mechanisms and by supporting journalistic investigations revealing the
sources and dissemination patterns of disinformation and highlighting the role of
government representatives in spreading disinformation. 185
Because disinformation is considered a wicked problem, some have called for new ways to
regulate the free flow of information with co-regulatory models. Some ideas were outlined
recently in the Disinformation as a wicked problem: Why we need co-regulatory frameworks
policy-paper from Brookings Institution. 186
To effectively manage disinformation and related online problems, governments and
platforms will need to develop an architecture to promote collaboration and build trust
among stakeholders. There are several models for multi-stakeholder collaboration,
among them the industry-led Global Internet Forum to Counter Terrorism (GIFCT) and
the government-led Information Sharing and Analysis Centers (ISACs). Those that prove
successful have in common continuous adaptation and innovation and a focus on trust-
building and information-sharing.

#7:
MESSAGING CAMPAIGNS
Messaging campaigns have provided a new front where disinformation can easily spread to
large amounts of people. Messaging campaigns refer to messages that contain false
information that pass through networks like Facebook Messenger, Twitter Direct Message,
and WhatsApp private and group messaging. These large-scale campaigns are difficult to
track because of the encryption security available on most messaging apps. Despite this
increased difficulty, there are new top-down and bottom-up approaches that are being
utilized to help stop the prevalence of messaging disinformation campaigns.
A few examples of resources counter-disinformation campaigns are included in Annex 3:
Emerging Solutions.
#8
LOCAL JOURNALISM SUPPORT
Bolstering local journalism is key to countering and preventing disinformation. Two pivotal
studies provide an evidence-based set of findings that show why support to quality,
independent media is key. One study notes that "results indicate local newspapers hold their
governments accountable, keeping municipal borrowing costs low and ultimately saving local
taxpayers money."187 A second study observed, "We find newspapers have a robust positive
effect on political participation, with one additional newspaper increasing both presidential
and congressional turnout by approximately 0.3 percentage points."18Furthermore, major
research undertaken by the United Nations and the International Center for Journalists cited
quality journalism as a major force for identifying and exposing disinformation, 189 citing that
the 'viral load' of disinformation will only grow if journalism continues to suffer death blows
inflicted by the (COVID-19) pandemic. The importance of good, quality local journalism as
the key to fighting false news and noxious content was nicely argued in a pair of articles
written by Emily Bell at the Tow Center for Digital Journalism at Columbia University's

media sources. Total global newspaper advertising revenue may lose about $23.8 billion in
annual revenues from 2012 to 2021. More than 10 percent of this decline, around $3 billion,
is an estimated loss of annual revenue for local news media around the world. 192 Television
news is still holding its own in places such as the Philippines; however, more than 80
percent of Filipinos say they now go online for their news and spend four of their 10 hours
online accessing social media. 193
In the vacuum created by the loss of local newspapers, the Brookings Institution finds that
readers turned to outlets covering national stories that may have strong partisan leanings or
concentrate on partisan conflict. 194 As a result, Brookings observed that "in places where
news consumers cannot balance their news diet with local alternatives, voters tend to be
more politically polarized."195 Understanding the value of local journalism and the challenges
it faces, some civil society organizations have committed themselves to revitalizing and
protecting local news etforts. Through providing funding, training, and other resources to
journalists and local outlets, organizations ensure that communities have sustained access
to information through a more local lens and without a dependence on large-scale,
potentially partisan media houses.

#9 TRANSPARENCY IN JOURNALISM
As the spread of disinformation online grows and even reputable news agencies have
mistakenly shared false information,there is a need for better trust and transparency
standards to hold media agencies accountable. Some very basic standards such as bylined
articles, public display of address and registration information, and disclosure of funding
sources and editorial board, for example, can assist readers to understand the sources and
reliability of the information they read. By developing standards for media agencies,
journalism will be held to greater account for what it publishes. Examples of ongoing
initiatives aimed at rebuilding trust and strengthening transparency in journalism are included
in Annex 3: Emerging Solutions.
#10 ADVERTISER OUTREACH
In order to disrupt the funding and financial incentive to disinform, attention has also turned
to the advertising industry, particularly with online advertising. A good example of this is the
concerted response to the discovery of the websites traced to the village of Veles outside of
Skopje, Macedonia, which showed how easy it was to exploit the digital advertising model to
flood the news ecosystem with fabricated content. Wired Magazine profiled the Veles case
study in 2017.199
As most online advertisers are unaware of the disinformation risk of the domains featuring
their ads due to the automated process of ad placement, they inadvertently are funding and
amplifying platforms that disinform.20° Thus, cutting this financial support found in the ad-tech
space would obstruct disinformation actors from spreading messaging online. Efforts have
been made to inform advertisers of their risks, such as the threat to brand safety by being
placed next to objectionable content, through conducting research and assessments of
online media content. Additionally, with this data, organizations hope to aim to redirect
funding to higher-quality news domains, improve regulatory and market environments, and
support innovative and sustainable models for increasing revenues and reach.
A few examples of advertiser outreach are included in Annex 3: Emerging Solutions.
Demand-Side Solutions
Other groups have centered their efforts on targeting the opposite side of disinformation, the
"demand." With demand-side solutions, the focus shifts to reducing the general societal
acceptance or tolerance of distorted and fabricated items.201 These approaches are often
viewed as more important for sustaining long-term impacts as they concentrate on why and
how disinformation influences society and the strategies to develop societal resilience
against it. Different demand-side solutions often look to governments, tech giants, and social
media companies to promote education and training, raise awareness, or advance other
efforts toward building more resilience against disinformation.

and advocacy on the vulnerability of countries to disinformation and exposure.
To build societal resilience against disinformation, the public must be aware of and
understand the issue. Public awareness campaigns serve to inform and educate

DIGITAL LITERACY & SECURITY
Civil society organizations have also sought to increase digital literacy and security skills to
empower the online community to identify and counter disinformation. Digital literacy
trainings provide lessons and resources for understanding how to identify, evaluate, and
compose information on digital platforms. This type of literacy expands understanding of how
to navigate, read, and interpret in a digital environment, as opposed to media literacy that
focuses primarily on understanding and interpreting journalism. Furthermore, digital security
initiatives produce and provide tools and behaviors for maintaining safety of personal
identities and information online that protect people and groups from becoming the target of
mis/disinformation.
An example is the Digital Society Project, which seeks to provide data on the intersection of
politics and social media. Topics include online censorship, polarization, misinformation
campaigns, coordinated information operations, and foreign influence in and monitoring of
domestic politics. It uses the Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) framework, also used by
USAID in Journey to Self-Reliance (JSR) metrics, to assess various digital issues including

Elections-focused programming efforts (both supply- and demand-side solution)
To defend the integrity of democratic elections worldwide, reducing disinformation has been
central to elections-focused programming in all these common goals:
• Building the capacity of election management bodies to combat disinformation during
electoral periods.
• Strengthening and adapting citizen election observation to incorporate disinformation
monitoring and exposure efforts.
• Adapting international election observation to integrate monitoring of the information
environment, including social media.
• Supporting independent media election coverage capacity and resources to increase the
supply of accurate information during elections.
•Increasing incentives for ethical online conduct by political parties and campaigns (such
as facilitating norms for online Codes of Ethics for political parties).
As socialmedia has changed how audiences consume and spread political information,
focus has shifted to monitoring the transformed information environment before and during
election periods. Emphasis has been placed on citizen election and campaign finance
monitoring, focusing on exposing disinformation on social media and other digital platforms
during election campaigns. Election management bodies (EMBs) tend to have significant
power to regulate speech and can set some ground rules. Media platforms have been
compelled by EMBs to be transparent about political advertising during an election season.
A report produced by the Kofi Annan Commission on Elections and Democracy in the Digital
Age puts forward recommendations to governments and internet platforms to safeguard the
legitimacy of elections. As the report notes, "For the foreseeable future, elections in the
democracies of the Global South will be focal points for networked hate speech,
disinformation, external interference, and domestic manipulation."202
Disinformation assessments have also been incorporated within international election
observation and management missions. With this, organizations have offered trainings and
guidance for election bodies and other stakeholders in regulating speech, campaign
violations, and the prosecution of violations.
A few examples of elections-focused programming and disinformation assessments are
included in Annex 3: Emerging Solutions.
There is also advocacy working to motivate social networking platforms, advertisers,
governments, and other parties to improve the information environment with pertinence to
the integrity of elections. In particular, advocacy aimed to achieve greater transparency in
political advertising, close fake accounts and bots, and de-monetize suppliers of
disinformation. An example of this is European Commission's "Code of Practice on
Disinformation," a self-regulatory Code of Practice to fight disinformation and ensure
transparent, fair and trustworthy online campaign activities ahead of the 2019 European
elections. Signatories included Facebook, Google, Twitter, Mozilla, Microsoft, and TikTok.203

to disseminate messages in adverse and media-saturated communities. An example of this

A. WHAT GOVERNMENTS CAN DO
Governments allocate state resources and execute strategies in order to protect their
citizens and the integrity of their information systems/democracy from the harms imposed by
information disorder. This proves difficult to accomplish through traditional, analog legislative
action because disinformation networks transcend the national borders where legislative
mandates are confined. We will examine below several countries that have attempted to
quell the production and dissemination of disinformation through legal and regulatory
Though it can be well-intentioned, criminalizing the spread of disinformation in digital spaces
presents even more negative ramifications for democratic governance. In countries where
disinformation legislation has been introduced, creating or sharing digital content and
information becomes risky and punishable. The resulting chilling effect ultimately hampers
democratic protections for a free press and the freedom of expression. Likewise, any whole
scale internet or platform shutdowns pose the same anti-democratic results while also
creating information vacuums within communities amid public health or safety crises. As
USAID negotiates the entangled, disinformation landscapes that intersect global and local
programming, programs should be wary both of legislative efforts to limit expression online
and internet/platform blackouts for the dangers they pose to democracy.
1. Whole-of-Government Approaches
There are very few examples of whole-of-government approaches (integrated activities of
government agencies increasing coherence in policy development on an issue) in the
disinformation space. Policymaking is likely to take time and will need to be significantly
informed by the private sector and civil society. Two examples in Scandinavia are discussed
to illustrate this approach.
Some governments have seen success in whole-of-government approaches in which
government agencies, social institutions, and civil society collaborate to collectively close the
digital, education, and social fissures that disinformation campaigns need to infiltrate media
and political landscapes.
In Sweden, for example, the whole-of-government approach (a comprehensive approach
that involves government, private and civil society sectors and media) attempts to be as
multi-faceted as the issue itself. Focused on maintaining the integrity of its electoral
processes, the Swedish government has poured resources into shoring up its electoral
infrastructure by safeguarding electronic voting machines and providing new training for civil
servants and voting officials. The government, electoral bureaus and cybersecurity agencies
have committed to forming an inter-agency cooperative to combat the issue.205 Sweden has
also focused on bettering public media literacy through enhancing high school curriculums
as a long-term strategy against information disorder. Lastly, five of the country's most
prominent media news outlets have created a scrupulous and highly visible fact-checking
collaboration to maintain the integrity of Swedish media and spread mutual oversight over
multiple media stakeholders.206 Sweden's approach has required weaving together
USAID.GOV

resources to defend the many susceptible ports of entry that misinformation and
disinformation penetrate in media landscapes and societies.
In Finland, response to the global information crisis has included a sweeping media literacy
education effort. In junior high and high schools, Finnish students use a digital literacy toolkit
in order to understand how to implement best practices in their own social media
engagement. In the world of electoral and media professions, Finland has dedicated
resources to disinformation trainings and workshops for civil servants and journalists.207 This
approach seeks use of public pedagogy and a more robust media literacy secondary
curriculum to intervene at every level of societal strata, in hopes that many small
contributions by individuals will add up to big structural changes that make a nation less
vulnerable to disinformation. Critics of the Finnish strategy call it too slow moving to address
such a fast-moving problem and worry that there are not concrete ways to measure its
success.208 Taiwan and Lithuania provide other good examples of whole-of-government
approaches to mis/disinformation. 209
2. Strategic communications and State coalitions
On a broader scale than the individual efforts of governments within their respective
countries, coalitions among states and policy stakeholders are expanding global efforts to
fight disinformation, such as EUvsDisinfo and the Atlantic Council.
The EUvsDisinfo is a flagship strategic communications project of the European External
Action Services, East StratCom Taskforce since 2015 to "increase public awareness and
understanding of the Kremlin's disinformation operations, and to help citizens in Europe and
beyond develop resistance to digital disinformation and media manipulation."210 EUvsDisinfo
has hands in three major areas to stymie global disinformation. The project conducts data
analytics of media spaces to identify and publicize disinformation campaigns started by the
Kremlin or pro-Kremlin media outlets; the data is archived in an open-source, dedicated
database that tracks disinformation around the world. The project also publishes summaries,
articles, and reports both within the research community and for wider general readership in
order to make a technical and complex issue accessible to the broader global communities it
impacts. Lastly, EUvsDisinfo engages with governments, media outlets, universities, and
civil society organizations by offering training resources to better prepare and problem-solve
around issues of information disorder.
Another example of strategic communications is The Atlantic Council, a "nonpartisan
organization that galvanizes U.S. leadership and engagement in the world, with allies and
partners, to shape solutions to global challenges."211 Among the numerous capacities
through which Atlantic Council conducts international work, their recently published
Democratic Defense against Disinformation 2.0 provides a current snapshot of global
disinformation campaigns at work, including proposed solutions, progress made, and
criticisms and recommendations made to the U.S. executive and judiciary branches
regarding urgent steps needed in the path toward a healthier information ecosystem.
3. Legal and regulatory measures
While there are examples of legal and regulatory measures intended to address
disinformation, the difficulty is that many are controversial because they also restrict freedom
of expression.

To achieve good legal and regulatory approaches to disinformation will require civil society
and independent media organizations to have a significant voice in policymaking through
multi-stakeholder collaboration. Governments face very real tradeoffs in developing
regulations on digital rights, disinformation and dangerous speech, while balancing
protections for freedom of speech, transparency, and privacy. Regime type is an important
variable to consider.
Guidance on good practices regarding regulation and policymaking in this area was put
forward by the UN SpecialRapporteur on Freedom of Opinion and Expression, the
Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) Representative on Freedom
of the Media, the OAS Special Rapporteur on Freedom of Expression and the African
Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (ACHPR) Special Rapporteur on Freedom of
Expression and Access to Information, with Article 19 and the Center for Law and
Democracy. These standards can be useful in evaluating legal and policymaking processes
and frameworks; some important ones are excerpted here from the section on Standards on
Disinformation and Propaganda:
a) General prohibitions on the dissemination of information based on vague and
ambiguous ideas, including "false news" or "non-objective information," are incompatible
with international standards for restrictions on freedom of expression, as set out in
paragraph 1(a), and should be abolished.
b) Criminal defamation laws are unduly restrictive and should be abolished. Civil law
rules on liability for false and defamatory statements are legitimate only if defendants are
given a full opportunity and fail to prove the truth of those statements and benefit from
other defenses, such as fair comment.
c) State actors should not make, sponsor, encourage, or further disseminate statements
which they know or reasonably should know to be false (disinformation) or which
demonstrate a reckless disregard for verifiable information (propaganda).
d) State actors should, in accordance with their domestic and international legal
obligations and their public duties, take care to ensure that they disseminate reliable and
trustworthy information, including about matters of public interest, such as the economy,
public health, security, and the environment.212

ways in which people communicate and share information. Because social media offers free,
open access to reach widespread global publics, discussions have turned to calling for the
platforms to respond to the online environments and issues they have created. More
specifically, focus has narrowed in on social media's automated algorithms that have
provided an easy and rapid mechanism for misinformation to spread and be amplified,
leaving truth to be buried amongst this free reach of falsehoods.214 Thus, critics argue that
social media platforms must take greater responsibility for themselves and increase platform
regulation and oversight and question whether self-regulation is sufficient.

power to change the way information flows online and to address the conditions they created

In considering how and by whom platforms should be held accountable, discussion extends
to platform governance. Robert Gorwa, a scholar from the University of Oxford, explains
platform governance as an "approach necessitating an understanding of technical systems

platforms govern or influence publics via their platform practices, policies, and affordances

forms of governance.
Currently, there are three governance "lenses" being utilized for thinking about social media
platform regulation and policy: 1) self-regulation, 2) external governance, and 3) co-
governance. The first lens represents the presently dominant mode of governance, a rather
laissez-faire relationship between governing institutions and social media companies, in
which the companies dictate their own platform improvements and transparency efforts. The
second lens encapsulates governments enacting legislation regulating social media
platforms. Lastly, the third lens seeks to provide greater democratic accountability without
severe disruption to the status quo. As noted earlier, the challenge with this approach is
striking a balance between combatting the spread of disinformation and harmful content
while also preserving free expression online. Proponents of this lens have proposed the
creation of specialty organizations, third-party adjudication systems, or ombudsman
programs that would act to address and investigate platform complaints as well as set ethical
frameworks and standards, among other tasks.219 Some examples are ICANN, a not-for-
profit, public benefit organization that regulates domain names, and the Internet Governance
Forum, which includes all stakeholders on governance questions in open and inclusive fora.

VII. PART SEVEN: TEN THINGS USAID AND ITS PARTNERS
CAN DO TO COUNTER AND PREVENT DISINFORMATION
As noted in the primer's introduction, information disorder is a wicked problem. Like other
seemingly insurmountable challenges, there is a need to tackle the problem in a number of
ways. Any solutions to the root causes of information disorder will need to work in concert
with other issues, such as better governance, cleaner elections, stronger accountabilitythe
whole spectrum of DRG issues. Simply put, disinformation is the big spoiler of all the DRG
issues. It's not just about doing one little thing, however; it's about a lot of little things, done in
an interactive, adaptive way and over a period of time.
Photo: ©2020 Shutterstock/Chanonnat Srisura
While it may not be possible to eradicate information disorder, doing nothing is not an
option. There are steps that must be taken to help alleviate the problem and ensure that the
progress and successes USAID has made around the world are not jeopardized.
Note: you will want to make your work as context specific as possible and do original,
diagnostic research to determine the best course of action for implementing more effective
strategies.
A. TEN STEPS FOR DEALING WITH DISINFORMATION
1) Conduct a disinformation diagnostic. Take stock of the information environment in your
country. The Public Affairs Section, the Bureau of Intelligence and Research, and/or the
Global Engagement Center at the State Department may have some information, often
on a smaller scale. The assessment could be part of a standalone media program or
integrated into larger governance programming. An assessment should understand
cultural notions attached to information legitimacy and norms for accepting the veracity
of information. Some regions are culturally preconditioned to be much more skeptical
(e.g., former Soviet republics) while others experience wide deference to authorities
(many Asian societies).
USAID.GOV
DISINFORMATION PRIMER | 59

An assessment would look for answers to the following questions.
a. What are the biggest threats/vulnerabilities for disinformation?
a. What are likely disinformation themes, aims, and main sources of
disinformation?
b. Who is most vulnerable to the disinformation being spread?
c. What are the common disinformation narratives?
d. Who are the main disinformation purveyors?
e. How does it spread across communities, and who are the most vulnerable?
b. What is the media ecosystem in your country like?
a. What is the makeup of mainstream media, including state, public service, and
private media as well as community media and alternative media?
b. What is the social media landscape like in your country, and what are the
most popular platforms (i.e., Facebook, Twitter, WhatsApp, etc.)?
c. What are the most common ways that different segments of the population
consume information?
d. Where do different people get their information? Is it online or through TV,
radio, print or peer-to-peer sources?
e. How do people access the internet? (mobile/desktop)
c. What is the media literacy landscape? What are the media literacy levels?
d. What is the rate of mobile and internet penetration?
e. What does current research say about the state and nature of the media and social
media,including levels of press freedom, internet freedom and any threats or
vulnerabilities that exist regarding access to information??27
2) Carry out actor mapping. Assess the key stakeholders who contribute in positive and
negative ways to the media and information ecosystem in your country.
a. Who are the malign actors?
b. Are there civil society organizations, associations, or institutions that seek to root out
disinformation, increase public awareness, engage in fact checking, or contribute in a
positive way to countering the disinformation problem?
c. Who are the allies, and who are the foes? Are there media, civil society, academics,
think tanks, businesses, or government agencies that you can work with?
d. Are there gaps in the actors (fact-checking or media development organizations, for
example), and could these gaps be addressed by partnering with international CSOs
or companies?
3) Support media literacy initiatives. Given the changing nature of mass media and news
and information consumption habits, youth as well as other segments of the population
benefit from opportunities to learn critical thinking skills and to acquire the knowledge to
spot disinformation and other aspects of information disorder. Participants of media
literacy programming can also serve as good boosters or spreaders of critical thinking.
USAID.GOV
DISINFORMATION PRIMER | 60

However, media literacy, like other aspects of knowledge and learning, requires "booster
shots" in which individuals learning about how the system works can get updated skills
and knowledge on new developments and techniques of media manipulation. Efforts to
get media literacy into the curriculum of primary and secondary schools on a broad scale
are considered best practice, but media literacy programs can be run through schools,
libraries, and other community-level partnerships, and they should be integrated across
subjects, as well as serve as part of a civic education curriculum. If possible, they should
also target a variety of age groups, from children to adults and seniors. As part of media
literacy efforts, include ideas and tactics for prebunking.
4)
Fund independent media and local public interest journalism. High-quality,
independent, local news is under threat. Endangered by changing business models, big
tech's domination of the digital advertising market, and pressures stemming from media
capture, concerns over press freedom, and the overall safety of journalists, the future of
news will require substantial investment and partnership with donors as well as
experimentation with different models and approaches. As advocated by the Knight
Foundation, one of the best forms of resilience against mis- and disinformation is
journalism. 228
5) Support media monitoring and fact-checking initiatives specifically. As shared by
Lithuania's Elves in their fight against the disinformation trolls, you cannot fight
disinformation with disinformation. You need to fight back with the truth and good
reporting. Local actors also need to know where and how disinformation is spreading.
This same sentiment is shared by leading journalists and experts on disinformation, who
argue that the best defense against the lies, propaganda, conspiracy theories, and other
bad information that is circulating is the truth.229 Truth, transparency, and facts are an
essential piece of fighting back against the wicked problem of information disorder.
Distortion of the facts is a moving target, so the ability to do fact-checking needs to be
sustained over time.
6) Stay up to speed. Disinformation is a growing field and threat, and there is a need to
stay current on new research and tools for identifying disinformation trends and threats
and to stay abreast of the different disinformation narratives that could undermine
USAID's work. While this requires sustained effort, the cost of inattention is too high if
ignored.
7) Support internet governance and digital rights initiatives. Digitalization and the
spread of internet technologies has already led to the next frontier of information access.
It has, unfortunately, also provided another way to prevent citizens from accessing
information. Criminals and politicians are known to muddy the waters and engage in
malign activities, often using the internet and the disinformation playbook to gain money
and power. Just as human rights advocates have argued that internet access is a human
right and that there is a fundamental right to access of information, there is also a right
not to be disinformed. The internet freedom and digital rights sector that USAID has
supported and partnered with around the world is a vital source of expertise and
collaboration in the fight against disinformation. Consider potential partnerships with
digital security trainers, digital forensic investigators, digital literacy specialists, internet
governance experts, and others who can work with your local USAID programs as part of

DRAFT -- Partnership Language for USAID - Facebook
USAID and Facebook seek to pursue a more formalized strategic partnership to advance our mutual
interests in developing countries around the world.
This partnership will be built on our shared values that respect the voice, dignity, rights and safety of the
communities and individuals that we serve.
The goal of this partnership will be to target USAID investments to its local partners and provide USAID
local partners with streamlined access to Facebook tools, training and trusted partner networks that
address information integrity and content that has potential to cause harm. The partnership would
potentially include:
• USAID identification and support of partners for access to research technologies: Process
and point of contact by which USAID partners can get access to Facebook's CrowdTangle
platform to inform the design of USAID-funded projects and understand public engagement of
content posted on Facebook and Instagram.
• USAID identification and support of partners for access to ad credits: Process and point of
contact by which USAID partners can apply for ad credits and toolkits to be more effective on
Facebook products to raise awareness and address shared problems (e.g. hate speech, violent
extremism, dis/misinformation, Covid-19, promotion of authoritative information etc.).
• USAID identification and support of partners for participation in partnership programs:
Process and point of contact by which USAID can refer local partners interested in participating
in Facebook's networks and programs including:
• International Fact-Checking Network (IFCN): to participate in third-party fact-checking
and verification programs and receive IFCN certification.
• Trusted Partners: to provide market knowledge, conduct harm assessments and identify
context-appropriate risk mitigation approaches.
• Info-Centers: participation in the generation of content to be highlighted on Facebook's
Info Centers (i.e Climate Science Info Center, Voting Info Center, Covid Info Center).
• Digital Literacy Initiatives.
• Identification of touch points at USAID and at Facebook for collaboration and coordination
on countries of concern:
• Sharing an annually updated list of countries of concern.
• Process and point of contact by which State/USAID and its partners can raise concerns
and get feedback related to the violation of Facebook's community values, policies, and
terms of service, including inauthentic behavior on the platform.
O
Point of contact on Facebook's Product Support Team to coordinate technical training for
USAID partners and answer questions on platform features, including authorization to
publish ads funded by USAID.
Point of contact on Facebook's Election Team to coordinate support related to voter
education, election observation and flag potential spoilers or destabilizers to the political
transition.

• Point of contact for Facebook's Information Hubs to refer local partners who are pushing
authoritative content on trending whole-of-society issues (e.g. Covid-19, climate change,
etc.) and looking to maximize their reach.
Acceptance of common language to build in information-domain interventions into
agreements.

Other summary
On Friday, September 8, 2023, the Fifth Circuit issued an order significantly narrowing the
scope of the preliminary injunction in Missouri v. Biden.
As a result, USAID is no longer prohibited from engaging in activities touching on content
moderation in concert with State.
The Fifth Circuit found the injunction to be vague and overbroad, vacated the majority of it,
narrowed it to apply only to the White House, the Surgeon General, CDC, and FBI and excluded
all other parties, including the State Department. The Fifth Circuit determined certain White
House, CDC and FBI officials' content moderation activities regarding COVID-19 disinformation
might have violated the First Amendment, but did not find sufficient evidence that the other
named defendants were likely to have done so.
Talking points for the committee folks
CONTENT MODERATION
Background: On July 4, 2024, a federal district court in Louisiana issued a preliminary
injunction in Missouri v. Biden prohibiting the State Department, several other federal agencies,
White House officials and anyone acting "in concert" with them from directly or indirectly
(through third parties or implementing partners) urging or pressuring social media companies to
remove or suppress "protected free speech." The injunction identified a few exceptions to this
USAID was not named in the injunction, but its activities were impacted in certain
circumstances, such as when USAID collaborated on activities with the State Department or

other federal agencies named in the injunction. State issued guidance regarding content
moderation activities. USAID was prohibited from engaging in content moderation activities in
concert with State or other parties named in the injunction. OUs were instructed to consult GC
for guidance.
On July 14, 2023, the Fifth Circuit granted a temporary administrative stay of the preliminary
injunction previously issued in the case of Missouri v. Biden. The stay remains in place pending
further orders from the court. Oral arguments were heard on August 10, 2023. GC is closely
monitoring the status of this case and will inform DRG of any changes. As a result of the stay,
DRG can resume activities that involve engagement with social media companies and can
coordinate with State on such matters, with some guardrails.
In short, USAID should continue to exercise appropriate caution in how it engages with tech
companies. Put your FOIA+ or litigation lens on.
More detail on the guardrails is provided below:
• Avoid "content moderation" - My understanding is that DRG does not anticipate
flagging to social media companies content for removal or increased scrutiny or
attention ( (e.g., posts by certain individuals or entities), but if it does occur, DRG
should only do it in the most limited and exceptional circumstances, and only in close
• Avoid or exercise significant caution regarding any discussions with social
media companies of their "content moderation" policies - Similarly, If DRG will be
reaching out to any social media companies to discuss their policies or approaches to
content moderation (e.g., encourage them to strengthen safeguards), please touch
base with GC prior to outreach. Cleared talking points are recommended.
Maximize use of cleared talking points for DRG led meetings -lf DRG will be
hosting meetings involving discussions with social media companies that might
directly or indirectly touch on content moderation, GC recommends preparing
agendas and talking points and clearing them with GC.
• Coordination - Confirm (if possible) that State L has cleared on/is aware of any
State-led joint State/USAID engagements with social media companies involving
discussions of "content moderation" - Talking points cleared by GC are
recommended. GC should also be consulted on any planned strategies to promote or
amplify any frameworks or documents to help reduce the risk that such efforts are
misconstrued as coercive. USAID should exercise additional caution in re-engaging
with State on any initiative involving "content moderation" which lacks a written
roadmap or overview for social media company engagement, cleared talking points, or

FAQ on Communications with Social Media Companies
On October 5, 2023, State issued additional guidance (23 STATE 108554) regarding
communications with social media companies in light of the Fifth Circuit's decision in Missouri v.
Biden. As a result of the decision, which significantly narrowed the injunction previously issued
in the case, USAID was no longer prohibited from communicating with social media companies
about content moderation in concert with State (or other parties). GC drafted this Frequently
Asked Questions (FAQ) document in October 2023 as an additional resource to help USAID
staff address common questions in light of the Missouri v. Biden litigation. The case, renamed
Murthy v. Missouri, was subsequently appealed to the Supreme Court and ultimately dismissed
on procedural grounds.
As a result of the Supreme Court's dismissal of the case, USAID now has a greater ability to
communicate with social media companies. In September 2024, light edits were made to this
guidance in light of the developments in the Murthy v. Missouri litigation and updated guidance
from the Administration.
Bureaus and Missions should continue to follow this GC FAQ document, which is consistent
with State and White House guidance. White House guidance encourages departments and
agencies toengage appropriately with technology companies in order to address grave threats
and not to be dissuaded by litigation like Murthy v. Missouri, from engaging in this important
work. It underscores the importance of avoiding action that could be perceived as coercion.
Similarly, State's guidance notes that State Department activities involving or pertaining to
social media companies should continue, but highlights that the United States Government
(USG) cannot significantly encourage or coerce social media companies to take content
moderation actions in violation of the First Amendment.
This GC FAQ continues to apply until otherwise revised or replaced. Bureaus and Missions
should continue towork closely with GC/RLO and contact Chioma Ayogu([contact omitted]),
Megan Metcalf ([contact omitted]) and Jahn Olson ([contact omitted]) with any questions
about this FAQ, specific scenarios, or upcoming engagements.
Q #1: Does State's guidance or the recent litigation in Murthy v. Missouri prohibit or limit
USAID's ability to use social media to promote its work?
A. No. USAID can continue to use official USAID social media accounts to publicize the
work of USAID, in compliance with ADS 558 (Use of Social Media for Public
Engagement).

Q #2: Is USAID prohibited from communicating with social media companies or working
on issues involving information integrity and resilience?
A. No. USAID can continue to work with social media companies in accordance with the
guidance provided here and in close coordination with GC/RLO.
The guidance is designed to help USAID continue its work to advance human rights and
protect freedom of expression online, consistent with legal mandates in the Foreign
Assistance Act of 1961 (FAA) and annual appropriations acts. This may include work to
support information integrity, digital democracy, election security, digital security and
media. For example, funds were specifically made available under Section 7032(g) of
the FY 2023 Appropriations Act (Division K of P.L. 117-328) to advance digital security
and counter disinformation in USAID partner countries in the manner described in the
2023 Joint Explanatory Statement (JES) under the heading Digital Security and
Countering Disinformation:
1. address digital security to enhance the safety of implementers and
beneficiaries;
2. support civil society organizations working to counter government
surveillance, censorship, and repression by digital means;
3. combat weaponized technology, including the misuse of social media;
4. prevent the digital manipulation of elections, electoral data, and critical
infrastructure; and
5. counter disinformation propagated by malign actors, including the
People's Republic of China (PRC) and the Russian Federation.'
Q #3: Is USAID prohibited from partnering with social media companies on activities that
do not involve content moderation?
A. No. USAID may continue to engage in these partnerships. A couple examples have
been included below:
i. Digital literacy bootcamps for university students in partner countries
ii. Ad buys on social media outlets to publicize USAID activities or programs
in partner countries
iii. Development of online tools that civil society can use to help address
development challenges or business sustainability
Q #4: What are some considerations to keep in mind when communicating with social
media companies in general or with respect to content moderation in particular?
A. USAIDemployees and contractors should only request content be removed, retained,
posted, or promoted consistent with the social media company's policies.

B. Avoid actions that could be considered "coercion" or "significant encouragement" to act
in accordance with USAID's wishes or content moderation requests. USAID employees
and contractors must refrain from taking any actions that can be reasonably interpreted
as pressuring social-media companies to remove or post content.
a. "Coercion" includes actions that could reasonably be interpreted as pressuring
social media companies to remove, retain, post, promote content or take other
action by threatening to punish them or implying possible punishment if they fail
to do as USAID requests.
b. "Significant Encouragement" includes actions that could be reasonably
interpreted as excessive entanglement in a social media company's decision-
making process or attempts to exert meaningful control over the social media
company's decision-making.
C. Clearly communicate that any action taken in response to a request from USAID is
voluntary.
D.
USAID employees and contractors must not be involved in or attempt to influence the
content moderation decisions of social media companies. They must avoid direct
involvement in the social media company's content moderation decisions or
entanglement in the social media company's independent decision-making. USAID staff
and contractors should not tell social media companies what to do or how to deploy their
resources (e.g., size, composition, or performance benchmarks for teams responsible for
content moderation).
E. USAID employees and contractors should only make content moderation requests
related to USAID staff,activities, or objectives. Exceptions to this approach must be
cleared with GC/RLO.
Avoiding Significant Encouragement or Coercion
Q #5: What are some examples of actions that could be considered "coercion?"
A. As highlighted in State's guidance, depending on the context, the following could be
considered "coercion":
• Public calls for action from the USG pressuring social media companies to
endorse or adopt various industry or international principles or standards or
implement certain standards or policies.
• Public statements from the USG urging social media companies to take specific
action regarding content moderation or publicly criticizing social media
companies for failing to do so;
• Public statements noting that social media should be held accountable for failing
to take action through fundamental reforms, such as regulatory action.
Q #6: What are some examples of actions that could be considered "significant
encouragement?"
A. As highlighted in State's guidance, depending on the circumstances, the following could
be considered "significant encouragement":
3

• Actions inside and outside meetings with social media companies that identity
certain posts as misinformation, identify options for labeling or addressing the
misinformation in the post and asking for amplification of approved content the
USG has determined are accurate.
• Enlisting the assistance of senior leadership at USAID to facilitate resolution of a
content moderation request.
• Repeated requests for social media companies to change their content
moderation policies, particularly where the requests do not end until the social
media company makes changes that satisfy the USG's concerns.
Content Moderation Requests
Q #7: Can USAID staff or contractors request removal of content that violates the Social
Media Company's terms of service/ use or policies?
A. Yes. Content moderation requests must be related to USAID staff, activities or
objectives. USAID employees and contractors may only contact social media companies
to request removal of content that violates the social media company's terms of
service/use. Exceptions to this approach must be cleared with GC/RLO.
Such content frequently includes the following types of content: violent or graphic
content, terrorist propaganda or support, harassment, spam, intellectual property
infringement, impersonation of USG officials or official USG accounts, or certain privacy
violations.
Q #8: How does USAID request removal of violent, harassing or other content that
violates the social media company's terms of service/use?
A. Outreach to request the removal of such content must follow the procedure outlined below.
1. Content of Request - The request for removal must be cleared by GC/RLO. The request
for removal must identify the content USAID is requesting be removed, include a
screenshot or direct link to the content and identify the terms of service or terms of use
that the content violates. In each case, the social media company will decide how to
respond to the request, in accordance with its policies. The request must not be coercive
in tone or imply adverse consequences for the social media company if the content is
not removed. The request cannot use examples of adverse consequences or
reputational risk experienced by other social media companies that failed to take action
to motivate or persuade the social media company to take action.
2. Means of Transmission - The request for removal must be transmitted to the social
media company using existing channels as identified in platform terms of service, terms
of use, or policies, unless the social media company directs use of a different process.
3. Escalation - The request for removal should be submitted and shepherded by an
appropriate POC or identified alternative POC. Concerns should be escalated in
accordance with the social media company's existing policies. Senior leadership in
USAID/W or Missions must not be engaged to help facilitate resolution of ongoing issues
4

unless requested by social media companies, particularly if they are not presenting new
previously undiscussed issues or information.
4. Follow Up Outreach - USAID may engage in appropriate follow-up regarding its content
moderation request after a reasonable period of time. If the social media company or
online platform specifies a time frame for response, subsequent follow up or status
checks must follow that time frame. Follow-up messages may flag changed conditions or
additional relevant information that may have come to light since the original message
was sent. Any appeals or requests for reconsideration of a content moderation decision
must follow the social media company's policy. If there is no appeals process then
USAID cannot further engage regarding that particular content moderation request.
Q #9: How does USAID request Removal of content that Poses a Threat to the Safety of
USAID Staff or Recipients of USAID Foreign Assistance?
A. USAID may request that social media companies remove content that creates a serious
threat to the safety of USAID staff or facilities, or to recipients of USAID funds.
In such cases, Mission staff should contact the RSO or the DS Office of Protective
Intelligence Investigations (DS/TIA/PII) at [contact omitted] and copy the EXO
for the Mission. USAID/Washington staff should contact the USAID Command Center at
[contact omitted]). The email should include a screenshot or direct
link to the content, an explanation of the threat posed, and information regarding the
[access or personal detail omitted]
Failure to coordinate with EXO and RSO prior to outreach to the social media company
may result in removal of the content before it can be recorded for further investigation,
and may impede or preclude subsequent law enforcement action.
Q #10: How does USAID request Retention of content?
A. All requests for retention of content must demonstrate that the content did not violate the
social media company's terms of service or terms of use. USAID staff must follow the
same procedures regarding means of transmission, escalation, and follow-up outreach
as for requests for removal.
Q #11: How does USAID request Promotion of content?
A. USAID and its partners should rely on existing channels and tools developed by the
social media company (e.g., paid boosting) to promote or raise awareness of USAID
funded or supported activities. USAID may develop partnerships or execute
memorandums of understanding (MOUs) or other non-binding agreements with social
media companies to amplify or promote USAID projects or activities. USAID should
ensure the "ask" or purpose of the partnership is clearly communicated. USAID should
not conduct outreach to social media companies on behalf of its partners to encourage

social media companies or online platforms to promote or post content unless it is part of
a partnership, MOU, or other non-binding agreement.
Q #12: Can multiple OUs or Missions send content moderation requests regarding the
same content or enlist the assistance of senior leadership to help underscore the
importance of the request or raise its profile?
A. No. OUs and Missions must follow the process outlined in this guidance. Senior
leadership cannot be enlisted to help raise the profile or facilitate resolution of a content
moderation request. OUs and Missions should coordinate where possible to ensure that
the social media company is not receiving an influx of requests regarding identical
content from multiple parts of USAID. Content moderation requests should be submitted
and shepherded by an appropriate POC or identified alternative POC.
Q #13: Can USAID staff or contractors contact social media companies to make content
moderation requests on behalf of recipients of foreign assistance or members of the
public?
A. USAID employees and contractors should only make content moderation requests
related to USAID staff, activities, or objectives. Members of the public should be
encouraged to contact the social media companies directly, rather than referring these
incidents to USAID for follow up or action. Exceptions to this approach must be cleared
with GC/RLO.
Q #14: Can USAID form partnerships with social media companies?
A. Yes. USAID may develop informal or formal partnerships or execute a memorandum of
understanding (MOU) or other non-binding agreement with social media companies to
amplify or promote USAID projects or activities or partner to address a development
challenge or otherwise meet development objectives.
Q #15: Can USAID staff or contractors convene events that involve discussion of 1)
common approaches taken by social media companies to safeguarding users, promoting
human rights online, information integrity, or content moderation as well as 2)
opportunities to strengthen these approaches by adopting or aligning with international
standards, principles or best practices?
A. Yes. USAID staff and contractors must coordinate closely with GC/RLO when convening
multi-stakeholder dialogues, listening sessions, or other public discussions that involve
discussion of common approaches taken by social media companies to safeguarding
users, promoting human rights online, information integrity, or content moderation as
well as opportunities to strengthen these approaches by adopting or aligning with
international standards, principles or best practices.
These discussions should not focus on any one social media company's policies nor
should they explicitly or implicitly encourage participants to advocate for changes in
policy to social media companies and should not significantly encourage social media

companies to take action regarding specific content. Additional caution should be
exercised if these dialogues or discussions include participants from social media
companies. Any questions for social media companies should be submitted prior to the
event and reviewed by GC/RLO and shared with social media company participants, if
possible. USAID must communicate that social media company participation in Q&A is
strictly voluntary.
Q #16: Can USAID staff or contractors have one-on-one discussions with social media
companies about their policies for supporting users or promoting human rights online?
A. Yes, but discussions with social media companies on the subject of their policies,
practices or approaches to safeguarding users or promoting human rights online or
opportunities to strengthen their policies by adopting or aligning with international
standards, principles or best practices may only occur in strict accordance with this
guidance and only in cases where it advances clear foreign policy objectives under the
FAA or other applicable law.
• USAID staff and contractors must make clear that participation is entirely voluntary, that
the conversations are intended to be informational only, that social media companies
are under no obligation to provide information or create new data sets or documents for
USAID, and that social media companies should not provide personally identifiable
information (PII) or non-public information to USAID.
•
If USAID staff or contractors plan to have ongoing discussions with social media
companies or advocate for changes to company policies or practices, they are
encouraged to develop a voluntary non-bindinginformal or formal partnership and
memorialize it via email, MOU or a similar document. The document should identify the
shared expectations and objectives.
• The agenda, talking points, and list of questions for these discussions must be
cleared by GC/RLO prior to any discussions. The talking points should clearly
communicate the purpose of the meeting, which should be informational only.
• Permissible topics of conversation include questions or clarifications regarding:
• Existing policies, procedures and staff responsibilities.
•
Metrics or trends
Policies, practices or approach and response to specific types of issues
(e.g., such as addressing technology facilitated gender based violence
(TFGBV))
• How current policies or procedures might address various problem sets
or issues of concern not expressly addressed in existing social media
company policy. USAID staff and contractors cannot identify specific
posts or specific users and include them as a topic of discussion.
• Discussions should be limited in scope, duration and frequency and should not
require significant expenditures of time or resources on the part of the social
media company. USAID staff and contractors should not tell social media
companies what to do or how to make staffing or resourcing decisions (e.g., size,

composition, or performance benchmarks for teams responsible for content
moderation). Requests for additional detail or information should not be
burdensome and should be limited to areas and issues that may be unclear.
Before engaging, USAID staff and contractors should determine the "tipping
point" when they will either discontinue discussions or pursue a voluntary non-
binding partnership with the social media company to tackle the issue in more
depth.
Q #17: Can USAID reach out to social media companies to resolve "customer service
issues" related to its posts? For example, what if USAID paid the social media company
to "boost" or increase visibility of its posts on social media platforms, but the proposed
posts are consistently rejected?
A. Yes, USAID can reach out to a social media company to resolve "customer service
issues" related to its posts using the social media company's existing channels or tools.
If there is no existing process or point of contact to resolve these issues for users,
USAID can develop partnerships with socialmedia companies to help better amplify or
promote USAID projects or activities, consistent with the guidance above. USAID can
also flag this as a general issue for users, but cannot imply that the social media
company is expected to develop a process for use by the USG.
Q #18: How do the guidance from State and USAID address or take into consideration
freedom of expression?
A. This guidance reflects USAID's longstanding commitment to protecting and promoting
freedom of expression, and free and independent media consistent with the United
States' responsibilities as a party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political
Rights, which protects freedom of expression, and the right to freedom of speech
protected by the First Amendment to the United States Constitution. In the United
States, freedom of expression - whether exercised offline or online - receives strong
protection. The First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution states that "Congress shall
make no law ... abridging the freedom of speech." The United States Supreme Court has
interpreted the right to freedom of speech broadly and has only identified a limited
number of narrowly defined categories of speech that do not receive First Amendment
protection.
In carrying out its development mission overseas in partner countries, in accordance
with the foreign policy objectives of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 (FAA), USAID
strives to amplify and extend the reach of the United States' most cherished values and
beliefs: human dignity, freedom, and equality. USAID's commitment to advancing and
protecting these values and beliefs, including freedom of expression, is reflected in the
Agency's programs and policies. Further, it is the policy of the U.S. government to
encourage social media companies to respect human rights, including freedom of
expression.

Concept: Promoting Information Integrity and Resilience Initiative (PRO-INFO)
I. Problem Statement
Mis/dis/malinformation has become one of the most enduring challenges of our time, affecting
democracy in the Global North and South. We are at a watershed moment in how we respond to
the threat of disinformation. If we do not come together as a community of democracies to shape
the enabling environment that best responds to disinformation and toaddress whole-of-society
approaches that put information integrity and resilience at the forefront of our strategies around
democratic renewal, we will lose the moment to ensure a human rights centered approach to
governance.
The problems center around four main issues. First, while current bilateral and multilateral fora
have made initial investments to address information integrity and resilience, no platform exists
to bring together countries from Global North and South along with stakeholders from the
private sector, content producers, civil society, and emerging technology companies to jointly
address this challenge. Similarly, no donor coordination platform has the ability to rally
development agencies to spur investment for this critical challenge and agree on how to develop
and implement responses that effectively respond to the issue. Third, greater investment is
needed at the country level to strengthen capacity building efforts and bring diverse stakeholders
to the table to respond to disinformation related challenges with appropriate localized context.
Fourth, gender-based disinformation, including disinformation and propaganda aimed at women,
Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trangender, Queer, Plus (LGBTQ+), immigrants/minority populations
and other marginalized groups, is a growing problem that undermines democratic principles and
values, drives a wedge between citizens, and fosters stigmatization.
II. Objectives, Key Components, and Illustrative Ideas
Vision of success: Building upon and expanding USG efforts to address information integrity
and resilience globally, the U.S. Agency for International Development and U.S. Department Of
State will: 1) strengthen existing multilateral and multi-stakeholder bodies to address information
integrity; 2) improve international donor coordination; 3) enable USAID Missions to strengthen
the provision of information integrity and resilience technical assistance; and 4) integrate
diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility standards and best practices into policy making and
technical assistance. These efforts will help to strengthen private - public-civic partnerships
and develop common solutions that are coordinated and that apply lessons learned on the
most effective measures to support information integrity and resilience. This initiative will
build on the recommendations from the S4D Information Integrity Cohort's efforts and aim to
actualize one of their key recommendations to convene and scale a sustained community of
practice focused on information integrity and resilience, and coordination.
Objectives: PRO-INFO will strengthen information integrity and resilience through the
following objectives and activities:
OBJECTIVE 1: Strengthen existing multilateral / multistakeholder engagements globally to
more effectively address disinformation through increased coordination among like-minded
governments, civil society, and private sector stakeholders across the Global North and South.
1

PRO-INFO will deepen linkages between and across State-Department-led diplomatic
approaches at the multinational level, USAID-led development solutions at the local levels, with
a particular emphasis on the Global South. These activities will enhance collaboration and
shared understanding around key legal norms, policies and regulatory issues.
Key Components Include:
• Strengthen, Coordinate and Engage Multiple Stakeholder Fora to Expand
Capacity: increasing investments in and additional support will help to expand the
capacity of three existing multi stakeholder and multilateral bodies so that they can build
out collective solutions, strengthen coordination, and exchange lessons learned to address
information integrity and resilience globally, including in the Global South, where
information challenges are particularly acute. An effectively coordinated approach
enables the U.S. to maximize impact, strengthen partnerships, and share principles and
investments (see figure 1)
• We propose that the U.S., led by the Department of State, join the new
Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD)'s "Mis/Dis
Resource Hub." Illustrative activities for this Hub could include: create a data
hub that includes governance policies and initiatives to address information
integrity and resilience; convene a government and multi stakeholder dialogue,
build an analytical center to create consensus around effective practices; engage
with civil society, private sector, and media experts to address policy
effectiveness; and create a stocktaking review of existing development. (See Tab
1 for more details on these activities).
In addition, with State and White House active participation, PRO-INFO would
deepen cooperation and engagement with other multilateral bodies that address
information integrity and resilience, most notably, the G7 Rapid Response
Mechanism (G7 RRM) and U.S.- EU Trade and Technology Council (TTC). This
will enable us

OBJECTIVE 2: Build on and expand donor coordination to support information integrity

USAID will encourage donor agencies and the private sector to increase and more effectively
allocate resources. Across this objective, USAID will help shape donor priorities through policy
dialogues and by identifying country-level lessons learned.
• Harmonize Approaches Across Governments: This activity will rally like-minded
governments and philanthropies to invest and fund activities to strengthen information
integrity and resilience, most notably in the Global South. USAID will seek to boost
donor coordination efforts at the OECD (through, for example, the Development
Assistance Committee, the Mis-Dis Hub, and/or Govnet) by establishing a platform for
donor coordination on information integrity and resilience, as described in the following
paragraph below. In addition, it will strengthen coordination within other multilateral
bodies that the U.S. participates in with donors, including the European Union and G7
countries.
• Ensure that the Cohort on Information Integrity Endures Post S4D2: In addition to
OECD DAC and the Hub, USAID will also seek to institutionalize the Summit for
Democracy Cohort on Information Integrity in order to establish a permanent platform
for coordination to address MDM. The body could be housed under a multilateral or
foundation entity and would provide a permanent home for like-minded partners who are
already actively addressing these issues-including current cohort members from like-
minded governments, civil society and foundations. Efforts would be made to expand
existing membership and to elevate the critical need for greater private sector
engagement. The Cohort would provide an important platform for members to identify
the most urgent information integrity issues, establish an order of priority for addressing
those issues, and promote greater investment of resources to tackle these priorities.
OBJECTIVE 3: Strengthen USAID's information integrity and resilience programming
through technical assistance, evidence and learning, and multi-stakeholder partnerships at the
local level.
USAID development activities complement Objectives 1 and 2 by incorporating best practices
into USAID programming. These efforts will focus on providing technical assistance and
funding to USAID partners on the ground at the regional level, as well as advancing evidence
and learning in this space.
Key Components May Include:
• Expand Effective Models, Technical Assistance, and Rapid Response Funding:
Building on successes and lessons learned from existing programs, USAID will develop a
suite of tools and services to support country level programming led by USAID Missions.
This component could include:
• Showcase "Model" Country and Regional Programs: USAID would draw
upon existing, successful USAID-supported programs, to identify and share
lessons learned and emerging practices with other USAID Missions, donors, or
civil society groups. USAID regional platforms could coordinate study tours and
regional exchanges to disseminate research as well as programmatic lessons
learned, provide technical assistance to bilateral missions, and foster private

sector partnerships with regional and multinational private sector entities. They
could also provide opportunities for private - public-civic partnerships at the
country level, to include partnering with local private sector entities to bring best
in class solutions to address information integrity and resilience. These include:
digital platforms, as appropriate, emerging technology solutions, advertising, and
strategic communications capabilities.
Expand Technical Assistance: USAID would expand technical assistance to
USAID Missions for design support or amendments to existing programming.
This would include support for comprehensive planning and design such as:
conducting local assessments and political economy analyses, drafting
contextually based program design and procurement documents, supporting
technical evaluations of programs, development monitoring and evaluation
baselines and ongoing tracking, feedback support for adaptation, and work
planning.
Provide advanced support for Localization, Adaptation and Scaling: USAID
would assist staff or local partners to co-create local adaptation of model
programs, and source the appropriate technical assistance needed for the
adaptation or new programming. Rapid Response support through this initiative
could fund small, innovative pilots to kick-start programs to address information
integrity and resilience for priority missions, and local civil society and private
sector partners.
• Strengthen Evidence and Learning: While USAID and partners have sourced key
lessons learned, it is important to improve evidence-based understanding of how MDM
affects and undermines USAID's democracy and human rights efforts, as well as the
efforts of other development sectors. Given the current disconnect between research and
practice, these activities will build consensus around a learning agenda, indicators of
measurement, and theories of change. USAID will build upon its global experience in
programming in the information integrity and resilience space to generate applied
learning products for dissemination among the development community. The following
resources and tools will be developed within USAID and can be shared with the OECD
Mis/Dis Resource Hub, G7 RRM, and the TTC for broader uptake and coordination.
This component will produce:
MDM Research Best Practices Guidebook: Building from the 2021 USAID
Disinformation/Misinformation primer and the assessment of current
programming, this guidebook will recommend a detailed set of approaches,
including analytic frameworks for data collection and aggregate information
integrity and resilience performance indicators. The guidebook will address a
range of operating contexts and program characteristics that will assist policy and
